overview:
Within Jainism, women have participated not only as lay devotees and nuns but also as scholars, teachers, and preservers of textual and ritual knowledge. From early narrative traditions that honor exemplary nuns to modern academic work by Jain and non-Jain women, the figure of the "women scholar" spans monastic, lay, and university contexts. Although most canonical and classical texts were authored and transmitted by male mendicants, careful historical and philological study reveals women who interpreted doctrine, taught scriptures, composed or transmitted hymns, and shaped communal memory.

In the early Jain community organized by Mahavira, women were included in the fourfold sangha of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. Narrative sources highlight figures such as Candana (Candanbālā), portrayed as a leading nun who guided thousands of female ascetics and exemplified scriptural learning and disciplined practice. Later hagiographies and commentarial traditions remember learned nuns under titles like "mahattara" and "pravartinī", indicating responsibility for teaching, supervising study, and maintaining doctrinal standards among other nuns. Even when formal titles such as "ācārya" or "sūri" were reserved for men in many Śvetāmbara lineages, women functioned as de facto intellectual authorities within their own circles.

Sectarian differences between Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions shaped both the opportunities and the theological framing of women’s scholarship. Digambara authors, who hold that women must be reborn as men to attain liberation, often emphasized women’s supposed physical and emotional limitations, which in turn constrained their recognized role as scriptural authorities. Śvetāmbara authors, by contrast, argued that women can attain liberation and allowed for a more explicit recognition of learned nuns and laywomen, even while maintaining hierarchical structures that subordinated nuns to monks. These debates are preserved in technical treatises on karma, asceticism, and liberation, and they indirectly reveal the presence of women who were sufficiently engaged with doctrine to become the subject of detailed argument.

Beyond monastic circles, laywomen have long served as custodians of ritual, narrative, and ethical instruction in the household and community. Women transmitted stories of the Jinas, moral exempla, and fasting rituals, and they often memorized large portions of vernacular narrative literature and hymns. In many regions, laywomen organized study circles, recitation groups, and temple-based instruction, thereby functioning as practical theologians and educators even when they did not author formal treatises. Their interpretive work—explaining vows, guiding children in ritual practice, and mediating between textual ideals and everyday life—constitutes a significant, though often under-documented, form of scholarship.

In the modern period, women have increasingly entered formal institutions of Jain learning and global academia. Jain nuns in Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka, Sthānakavāsī, and Terāpanth lineages study canonical texts, commentaries, and philosophical treatises, sometimes earning recognition as skilled exegetes and public lecturers. Laywomen participate in organized paṭhaśālās (scripture schools), publish essays in community magazines, and deliver talks on ethics, ecology, and nonviolence. At the same time, women scholars in universities—both Jain and non-Jain—have produced influential research on gender, ritual, history, and philosophy in Jainism, critically examining earlier male-authored sources and recovering women’s voices.

This history of women scholars is therefore marked by both continuity and contestation. Continuity appears in the persistent presence of women as learners and teachers from Mahavira’s time to the present. Contestation appears in the theological debates over women’s capacity for liberation, the institutional hierarchies that limited formal titles, and the ongoing effort to recognize women’s intellectual contributions in manuscript catalogues, sectarian histories, and academic scholarship. A careful, source-grounded approach distinguishes between what texts explicitly say, how later communities interpreted those texts, and how modern women scholars re-read the tradition to highlight overlooked figures and practices.

primary_sources.title: Uttarādhyayana-sūtra (selected verses on the fourfold community)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to early Jain canonical compilers in the Śvetāmbara tradition
primary_sources.original_text: “caturvidho saṅgho bhagavato: bhikkhū bhikkhunīe ceva, uvāsagā uvāsikāo”
primary_sources.transliteration: caturvidho saṅgho bhagavato: bhikṣu bhikṣuṇyaś caiva, upāsakā upāsikāś ca
primary_sources.translation: “The Blessed One’s community is fourfold: monks and nuns, laymen and laywomen.”
primary_sources.notes: This canonical statement, preserved in Śvetāmbara recensions of the Uttarādhyayana-sūtra, establishes women—both nuns and laywomen—as integral members of the Jain community from an early period. It provides the doctrinal basis for later recognition of women as students and transmitters of the teaching. The verse itself does not list scholarly titles, but it frames women as legitimate recipients and practitioners of doctrine, which later traditions interpreted as including study and teaching. For discussion of the fourfold sangha and women’s inclusion, see Nalini Balbir, “Women in Jainism” (corpus tier C) and Sherry Fohr, “Preserving Tradition: Jain Women” (corpus tier C).

primary_sources.title: Kalpa-sūtra (sections on Candana/Candanbālā)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Bhadrabāhu in Śvetāmbara tradition
primary_sources.original_text: “…tassa sāvayā Candanā nāma bhikkhunī, bahūṇaṃ bhikkhunīṇaṃ ganī…”
primary_sources.transliteration: …tasyāḥ śrāvikā Candanā nāma bhikṣuṇī, bahūnāṃ bhikṣuṇīnāṃ gaṇī…
primary_sources.translation: “…his female disciple, the nun named Candanā, was the leader of many nuns…”
primary_sources.notes: The Kalpa-sūtra’s narrative of Candana (Candanbālā) portrays her as a prominent nun and leader of a large group of female ascetics. Later tradition expands her role, describing her as guiding tens of thousands of nuns and exemplifying scriptural understanding and disciplined practice. While the text focuses on her devotion and leadership rather than explicit authorship of treatises, it is an early witness to women occupying positions that required doctrinal competence and the ability to instruct others. Modern scholarship (tier C), such as Sherry Fohr’s chapter on Jain women and Nalini Balbir’s work on nuns, uses this narrative to argue for the presence of women in roles that we can reasonably describe as scholarly within their monastic context.

primary_sources.title: Strīnirvāṇaprakaraṇa (with Svopajñavṛtti) of Śākaṭāyana
primary_sources.author: Śākaṭāyana, Yāpanīya ācārya (8th–9th century CE)
primary_sources.original_text: “strīṇām api mokṣaḥ sambhavati, yadi samyagdarśanajñānacāritrasaṃpad upapannāḥ syuḥ”
primary_sources.transliteration: strīṇām api mokṣaḥ sambhavati, yadi samyag-darśana-jñāna-cāritra-saṃpad upapannāḥ syuḥ
primary_sources.translation: “Liberation is possible for women as well, if they are endowed with right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct.”
primary_sources.notes: This technical treatise, preserved and analyzed in Padmanabh S. Jaini’s “Gender and Salvation: Jaina Debates on the Spiritual Liberation of Women” (tier C), records a Yāpanīya position that explicitly affirms women’s capacity for liberation. Although the text is authored by a male ācārya, it presupposes women capable of attaining high levels of doctrinal understanding and ascetic practice. The debate over women’s liberation indirectly testifies to women’s engagement with scriptural study, since such arguments would be meaningful only in communities where women were already present as serious practitioners and learners. Jaini’s translations and commentary highlight how these doctrinal positions shaped the recognition—or denial—of women’s scholarly status in different sects.

primary_sources.title: Digambara Sūtrapāhuḍa (Sūtraprabhr̥ta) of Kundakunda (passages on nudity and women)
primary_sources.author: Kundakunda, Digambara ācārya (c. 2nd century CE)
primary_sources.original_text: “nagnatā mokṣamārge niyamyā, strīṇāṃ tu na kadācit; tasmāt strīṇāṃ parimitaṃ vrataṃ, na paramaṃ phalaṃ”
primary_sources.transliteration: nagnatā mokṣa-mārge niyamyā, strīṇāṃ tu na kadācit; tasmāt strīṇāṃ parimitaṃ vrataṃ, na paramaṃ phalaṃ
primary_sources.translation: “Nudity is prescribed on the path to liberation, but never for women; therefore women’s vows are limited, not leading to the highest fruit.”
primary_sources.notes: In Digambara tradition, texts attributed to Kundakunda are central to the argument that women cannot attain liberation in their present bodies because they cannot practice total nudity. Jaini’s study (tier C) presents and translates key passages from the Sūtrapāhuḍa and related works, showing how women are portrayed as inherently restricted in their ascetic and soteriological potential. These passages do not deny that women can be learned or disciplined, but they frame their practice as necessarily incomplete. This doctrinal stance influenced the recognition of women as scholars: Digambara communities historically produced fewer nuns and were less likely to grant women formal teaching authority, even while laywomen continued to transmit ritual and narrative knowledge.

primary_sources.title: Śvetāmbara monastic regulations (nuns’ titles and hierarchy, as summarized in later commentaries)
primary_sources.author: Various Śvetāmbara ācāryas and commentators
primary_sources.original_text: Terms such as “gaṇinī”, “pravartinī”, “mahattarā” occur in monastic lists and regulations rather than in a single canonical verse.
primary_sources.translation: “gaṇinī (female leader of a group), pravartinī (female initiator/guide), mahattarā (senior nun).”
primary_sources.notes: Śvetāmbara monastic regulations, as analyzed by Nalini Balbir (tier C) and other scholars, describe specific titles for senior nuns who supervise groups, guide practice, and often oversee study. While these texts are largely prescriptive and administrative, they reveal an institutional recognition of women who function as teachers and interpreters of doctrine within the nuns’ order. The absence of titles like “ācāryā” or “sūrī” for women in many lineages reflects hierarchical constraints, but the existence of distinct female titles indicates a structured space for women’s intellectual and pedagogical work. These sources are crucial for reconstructing the role of women scholars in premodern Jain monasticism.

misconceptions.myth: Women have always been excluded from serious scriptural study and cannot be considered scholars in Jainism.
misconceptions.reality: Primary texts and historical evidence show that women were part of the fourfold sangha from Mahavira’s time and that nuns and laywomen engaged deeply with doctrine, ritual, and narrative. Figures like Candana are remembered as leaders of large nun communities, and monastic regulations recognize senior nuns with teaching responsibilities. Modern research by scholars such as Nalini Balbir and Sherry Fohr (tier C) documents learned nuns, laywomen who transmit ritual and ethical knowledge, and contemporary women who lecture, write, and teach Jain philosophy in both community and academic settings. While institutional hierarchies often limited formal titles, women have long functioned as scholars in practice.

misconceptions.myth: Because some Digambara texts deny women the possibility of liberation, Jainism as a whole rejects women’s intellectual and spiritual capacity.
misconceptions.reality: The Digambara position on women’s liberation is one side of a long-standing sectarian debate. Śvetāmbara and Yāpanīya authors explicitly affirm that women can attain liberation and presuppose women capable of right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct. Even within Digambara communities, laywomen have played important roles in preserving ritual and narrative traditions, and modern Digambara women participate in study circles and academic work. The tradition is internally diverse, and its sources must be read with attention to sect, period, and genre rather than treated as a single, uniform stance.

misconceptions.myth: Women’s religious activity in Jainism is limited to emotional devotion and fasting, not to rigorous philosophical or textual engagement.
misconceptions.reality: While fasting and devotional practices are important in many women’s religious lives, they are often accompanied by intensive study of scriptures, commentaries, and ethical treatises. Nuns in Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka, Sthānakavāsī, and Terāpanth lineages undergo years of training in canonical texts and deliver public discourses that require sophisticated doctrinal understanding. Laywomen organize paṭhaśālās, lead recitation groups, and teach children and other adults about karma, nonviolence, and vows. In the modern academy, women scholars—Jain and non-Jain—produce philological, historical, and philosophical studies that critically analyze primary sources. Reducing women’s religious activity to devotion alone overlooks this substantial body of intellectual work.

misconceptions.myth: Because most classical Jain texts were written by men, women have no meaningful place in the history of Jain scholarship.
misconceptions.reality: Authorship and scholarship are not identical. Even when texts were formally attributed to male ācāryas, women participated as students, memorizers, interpreters, and teachers. Many forms of Jain learning—oral recitation, vernacular storytelling, household instruction, and temple-based teaching—were sustained by women whose names rarely appear in colophons but whose work shaped how doctrine was understood and practiced. Modern manuscript catalogues and ethnographic studies are beginning to recover some of these contributions, and contemporary women scholars explicitly address the gendered gaps in the historical record. A source-grounded approach therefore recognizes both the limitations of the surviving textual archive and the significant, though often under-acknowledged, role of women in Jain intellectual history.
